questions.q: In the lexicon scorer, what does the negation rule do?
options: It deletes every review that contains 'not'
It flips the sign of a word that directly follows a negator such as 'not', 'no', 'never' or 'hardly'
It doubles the score of every negative word
It replaces negators with the word 'bad'
questions.explain: The scorer checks whether the previous token is a negator and, if so, flips that word's polarity, so 'not bad' counts as positive.

questions.q: 32 of the 80 test reviews scored exactly 0 with the lexicon. What does this reveal?
options: The lexicon has low coverage: those reviews contain none of its words, even when the sentiment is obvious to a human
Those reviews are truly neutral
The negation rule is broken
The test set contains duplicates
questions.explain: A score of 0 usually means no lexicon word matched, not neutral sentiment. Reviews like 'It exceeded my expectations' use words the lexicon does not contain.

questions.q: The classifier scored 0.98 in cross-validation on the training data but only 0.70 on the 80 hand-written reviews. What is the best explanation?
options: Cross-validation is always more accurate than a real test
Logistic regression cannot classify sentiment
The training reviews all came from the same few templates, and many test words were never seen in training
The test set was too large
questions.explain: Cross-validation only measures performance on data like the training data. Independent, differently worded reviews expose the vocabulary gap: about 59% of the test words were unseen.

questions.q: Why is 'Oh great, it broke on day one' hard for both approaches?
options: It contains too many words
It is sarcastic: the positive word 'great' is meant negatively, and word counts cannot see the tone
It contains a URL
Sentiment models only work on sentences with fewer than five words
questions.explain: Sarcasm reverses the literal meaning of words. In the lexicon, 'great' and 'broke' cancel to a score of 0; the classifier stays near 0.5.

questions.q: What is the responsible way to use a pretrained sentiment tool such as VADER or a transformer model?
options: Trust the published accuracy and skip testing
Only use it on data in the same language as your favorite example
Retrain it on your first ten reviews
Evaluate it on your own labeled examples and inspect its mistakes before relying on it
questions.explain: Domain, wording and tone differ between datasets, so a tool's performance on your text has to be measured, and failures inspected, whichever approach you choose.
